text: MONDAY, JUNE 1, 1925.

label: paragraph_title
text: KIDNAPPING CASE

label: text
text:
The sequel to the alleged kid-
napping of Mr. Harry Pollitt,
secretary of the Communist or-
ganisation known as the National
Minority Movement, was heard
at Liverpool. Assizes before
Mr. Justice Fraser.
Five local men, William P.
Cochrane, 30, garage proprietor;
George F. McGachen, 30, cotton
salesman; James B. Owen, 30,
commercial traveller; James H.
Browner, 35, tailor; and John H.
Rowlandson, 26, commercial
traveller, were charged with con-
spiring to assault and unlawfully
imprison. Pollitt.

label: text
text: Mr. A. E. Griffith, who prosecuted, said that Mr. Pollitt, a boilermaker by trade and a trade union speaker, professing Communist beliefs and opinions, was to have addressed a meeting in Liverpool on Sunday, March 15. On the Saturday he was met at Edgehill Station, Liverpool, put into a motor care, and taken to the Liver Hotel, Rhyddalog, a village on the Flintshire moors.

label: text
text: Mr. Pollitt stated that at Edge-hill Station Rowlandson and Owen entered the railway compartment where he was and asked him to address a meeting at Marnaduke-street at the Communistist headquarters. He refused, but was pulled out of the train.

label: text
text: He was, he said, bustled through the barrier into a waiting motorcar. He made no protest at the hotel. He was asked what his financial loss had been, and he replied that he had suffered none. He did not accept any payment.

label: paragraph_title
text: FAME AND ADVERTISEMENT.

label: text
text: Cross-examined by Sir Henry Curtis Bennett, K.C. (defending), Mr. Pollitt said he was a Communist speaker and had been convicted in 1921 for making alleged seritious speeches.

label: text
text: Sir Henry: "In fact, I might describe you as the famous Mr. Politt -Yes, and I am only quite young."

label: text
text: Do you find advertisement is something which is apt to make you become famous?—No. I find one becomes famous and then gets advertisement.

label: text
text: When Mr. Pollitt described how he was pushed into the motor-car with five other men and said one of them sat on his knee, Sir Henry Curtis Bennett asked: "In an ordinary Ford car, with six persons, somebody had to sit on somebody's knee?" "Yes," replied Mr. Pollitt, "but I don't see why it should have been my knee."

label: text
text: How did you recognise that these gentlemen were not comrades directly they came into the compartment at Edgehill?—First, because I had a definite understanding with my comrades to meet me at Lime street; and, second, my comrades never meet me dressed as hooligans with their caps down over their eyes, mufflers on, and their coat collars turned up. (Laughier.)

label: text
text: Regarding a bottle of mustard oil with which Mr. Pollitt's chest was rubbed at the inn because he had a cough, Sir Henry asked: "Was it famous because some of it got on your chest?"

label: text
text: Mr. Pollitt: Rowlandson rubbed my chest with it—and did it very well.

label: header
text: THE CHINA MAIL.

label: text
text: You were quite friendly with the defendants?—No, I was diplomatic. Did you toss for drinks with them and lose?—No.

label: paragraph_title
text: DIPLOMACY.

label: text
text: Did you have everything you wanted, a glass of beer with your launch and so on?—Everything was quite proper.

label: text
text: Sir Henry suggested that far from declining financial assistance to recoup him for any loss, Mr. Pollitt received five £1 notes from the defendants.

label: text
text: Mr. Pollitt: I say it is a deliberate and dastardly lie. I had only $35s_{1}$ If I had had more I should have gone straight to Liverpool and exposed the whole business.

label: text
text: Mr. Bold, proprietor of the Liver Inn, said they appeared to be a happy party, and there was no sign that anyone was being detained against his will; and another witness said they behaved as if they were "all pals together."

label: text
text: Rowlandson stated in evidence that what took place was not ordered from the London headquarters of the British-Fascisti. At Edge-hill Station Mr. Pollitt made no protest. When the car broke down on the way to Shrewsbury, he gave Mr. Pollitt five £1 notes.

label: paragraph_title
text: BETTER THAN A SPEECH.

label: text
text: Sir Henry Curtis Bennett, addressing the jury, described some of the allegations of Mr. Pollitt as "beautiful bits of colour put into the case, which was being brought to see whether Englishmen could get justice."

text: Directly Mr. Pollitt realised what was going on, he said, Mr. Pollitt agreed, and saw perhaps a far greater advertisement in the alleged kidnapping than any speech he could have delivered in Liverpool.

label: paragraph_title
text: LESSER KNOWN PARIS.

label: text
text: Paris, to the majority of holiday makers, is only synonymous with Montmarre restaurants and the grey-upholstered Louis. Selze salons of the couturier, says the Paris correspondent of the "Morning Port." The shopping facilities of the Bon Marche will be the only reason for crossing the Selne, so they may even miss the Tuileries Gardens, not yet in the full splendour of their summertime herbaceous borders, or the Luxembourg terrace, where the pink and white hawthorn trees coquet with the grey stone statues of the long dead queens.

label: text
text: Will any one of the Easter visitors, I wonder, go so far away from such "dancings" as the "Garden of my sister" as to stroll through that old-world country town in the very heart of Paris called the Ile St Louis, and lean on the sunny stone coping of the qual to admire the house with gilt dolphin drainpipes to which perf little de Lauzun is said to have taken Le Grande Mademoiselle after their ill-assorted marriage.

label: text
text: The island takes its name from the saintly king who was the central figure of Thirteenth Century life in France. Paris, having been spared a great fire like the one that made Evelyn mourn "London was, but is no more," preserves an astonishing number of mediaevel buildings that few tourists ever see. Of these the best known is the most beautiful, the Sainte Chappelle, that "Most perfect monument of pure Gothic in Europe."

label: paragraph_title
text: CRUCIFIXION RELICS.

label: text
text: Louis IX. commissioned Pierre de Montorcau to build him this jewelled casket as a shrine to hold the crown of thorns, the fragment of the Cross, and the metal of the lance that pierced the side of Christ, that he had bought for 100,000 francs from the needy Oriental Emperor Baudoin.

label: text
text: Another great monument to St. Louis is the Sorbonne, the great centre of French University life, in the rue de la Sorbonne, a street that has changed its name many times in the elastic French fashion since it was called the "Street of the Two Doors," in 1250.

label: text
text: The name of the college is always associated with that of Robert de Sorbonne, the almonter of St. Louis, whose disputes with that faithful Boswell, the Sire de Joinville, were among the monarch's few diversions. But it was Robert de Duai, the doctor of Queen Marguerite de Provence, who was the real founder of the Sorbonne.

label: text
text: He left a legacy with which Robert de Sorbonne started the little theological college that later, under the fostering care of Richelieu, grew into the vast building of to-day.

label: text
text: There is yet another institution, still existing in Paris, and more directly due to St. Louis's benign, violence, with a history so curious and interesting that its neglect by the majority of guide-books is "all the more inexplicable".

label: paragraph_title
text: 300 ULIND BEGGARS

label: text
text: There is no trace now left in the rue St. Honore of the original Hospice of the Quinze-Vingts, the huge caravanseral where St. Louis, lodged his three hundred blind beggars with the double object of giving them shelter and riding the streets of them. The tobacco shop of L. Civette is just where the old gateway stood till Cardinal de Rohan realised in 1779 how valuable the site had become, and how much money he could realise by its sale.

label: text
text: Six years before the tragic folly of the necklace affair was to shake the throne of France, the Cardinal moved the blind beggars to the old hotel of the Black Mosquitaires, a corps that had been disbanded four years previously, and in this second home, built by de Coite in 1609, their bret ren live to this day in the rue de Charenton, far from the path of the tourist.

label: text
text:
St. Louis's dry much nearer the Grands Boulevards, but its days are doubtless numbered. Almost from the windows of that most dingy of little restaurants, on the corner of the rue Canbon and the rue St. Honore, where you may be served with food that might be equalled, but never surpassed, may be seen a deserted building that looks as if it had not been entered for many a day. Few people could tell more than that it formed part of the convent of the Dames de l'Assomption, that once stood where the big new building of the Cour des Comptes is now, but the old house is, or was a few months ago, a link with the Thirteenth Century in modern Paris.
